title: Bright light and mental fatigue: Effects on alertness, vitality, performance and physiological arousal
research_question: To investigate whether a higher illuminance level (1000 lx vs. 200 lx at the eye) particularly benefits individuals who suffer from mental fatigue (not sleep pressure, but mental exertion) on self-report measures, task performance, and physiological arousal. Additionally, to investigate whether individuals' mood, appraisals of lighting, experience of space, and beliefs concerning lighting effects on performance and mood differed as a function of lighting condition and mental state.

participants.description: Students (12 male, 16 female), mean age 23 (SD=4.1, range 19-39). None were extreme chronotypes or had eye/general health complaints. Study took place in Eindhoven.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but likely university students.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Office lighting condition: 1000 lx at eye level (1040 lx at work plane, 8.70 × 10^14 photons*s-1*cm-2, 330 μW/cm²) with 4000 K CCT and CRI Ra=86.
Office lighting condition: 200 lx at eye level (280 lx at work plane, 1.80 × 10^14 photons*s-1*cm-2, 68 μW/cm²) with 4000 K CCT and CRI Ra=86.
Mental fatigue induction: 9-min Multi-Attribute Task Battery (MATB) and 20-min modified Stroop task (incongruent trials).
Control condition (rested): 9-min nature movie, 17-min leisure magazines, and 3-min congruent Stroop task.

mechanisms: Arousal-level theories (Yerkes-Dodson Law) suggesting an optimal illuminance level for task performance based on task difficulty, where high bright light might improve simple tasks but worsen complex tasks.
Replenishment of mental resources and self-control capacity by bright light, particularly when individuals are in a fatigued state.
implementation_implications: It is too early to recommend widespread installation of intense general lighting schemes solely to increase alertness and vitality, given mixed performance effects and potential adverse appraisals when rested.
Individuals needing temporary mental restoration at work should seek exposure to daylight (indoors near a window or outdoors during a short break).

limitations: Baseline differences in some subjective and performance measures existed despite efforts to minimize them, requiring baseline scores as covariates.
The light exposure duration was relatively brief (half an hour), and post-exposure effects were not measured, limiting conclusions about persistence.
EEG or fMRI were not employed, preventing measurement of temporal or spatial modulations in brain activity.
Only two light manipulations (200 lx vs. 1000 lx) and a limited set of performance tasks were used, limiting generalizability of optimal illuminance levels for different tasks.
Tasks were presented in a fixed order (PVT, then Go-NoGo, then 2-Back) without rest periods, potentially leading to order effects or task engagement influencing subsequent task performance.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to bright light, particularly in the blue spectrum, can directly enhance alertness and cognitive performance by influencing the non-visual photoreceptive system.

mechanism_chain.description: Bright light exposure leads to physiological changes that increase alertness.

instruments_used.name: Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS)
instruments_used.description: A 9-point self-report scale measuring subjective levels of sleepiness.

instruments_used.name: Multi-Attribute Task Battery (MATB)
instruments_used.description: A computer-based task battery simulating a supervisory control environment, used for both fatigue induction and performance measurement.

instruments_used.name: Modified Stroop Task
instruments_used.description: A variant of the classic Stroop task, used for mental fatigue induction and assessment of cognitive interference.

instruments_used.name: Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT)
instruments_used.description: A simple reaction time task used to measure sustained attention and vigilance.

instruments_used.name: Electroencephalography (EEG)
instruments_used.description: Measures electrical activity of the brain, often used to assess changes in alpha and theta power related to alertness and fatigue.

instruments_used.name: Heart Rate Variability (HRV)
instruments_used.construct: physiological arousal, autonomic nervous system activity
instruments_used.description: Measures variations in the time interval between heartbeats, reflecting autonomic nervous system activity and physiological arousal.
